'''Tele-snaps''' (often known as '''telesnaps''') were off-screen photographs of British television broadcasts, taken and sold commercially by '''John Cura'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> (born Alberto Giovanni Cura in [[Clapham]], [[South London]], England; 9 April 1902 – 21 April 1969). From 1947 until 1968, Cura ran a business selling the 250,000-plus tele-snaps he took. The photographs were snapped in [[Half-frame camera|half of a normal frame]] of [[35mm format|35mm film]], at an exposure of 1/25th of a second. Generally around 70–80 tele-snaps were taken of each programme. They were mostly purchased by actors and directors to use as records and examples of their work before the prevalence of [[videocassette recorder]]s.

For many early programmes tele-snaps are the [[List of lost television broadcasts|only surviving record]] of their appearance. From the 1990s onwards, tele-snaps have often been used by groups of fans to recreate [[Doctor Who missing episodes|lost ''Doctor Who'' episodes]], creating "reconstructions" by marrying the images to fan-recorded off-air soundtracks of the episodes.

==History==
[[File:OOTU Telesnaps.jpg|frame|right|A sequence of tele-snaps from the missing ''[[Out of the Unknown]]'' episode "The Prophet"]]
From an early age, Cura had been interested in electronics and photography, developing a reputation among his family as a "[[Heath Robinson]] inventor".<ref name="Lewisohn">Lewisohn, ''John Cura: Snapshots of History''</ref> In June 1946, the [[BBC]] resumed its [[BBC Television|television service]] following the hiatus imposed by the [[Second World War]]. Cura, recently [[demobilised]] from the [[Royal Air Force|RAF]], combined his twin passions of photography and electronics and began to experiment with developing a camera that could take pictures from a television screen. He eventually came up with a mechanism that took half-frame 18×24 mm images on 35 mm film (i.e. the same format as in 35 mm motion picture cameras), at a speed of 1/25th of a second.

Once satisfied with his process, Cura wrote to the BBC on 11 September 1947 enclosing samples of his work and requesting permission to exploit the images commercially. Cura's request caused considerable consternation in the BBC's legal department who were concerned about [[copyright]]. Ultimately, the BBC concluded that a television image was not covered by existing copyright law and replied to Cura giving him permission to proceed but to "only photograph the television image of individual artists who have instructed you to do so prior to their television appearance", and not to "give or sell the photographs to anyone other than the artist in question".<ref>Bignell, ''John Cura – Photographer of the Lost Archive'', p. 12.</ref> Cura often ignored this restriction, however, frequently sending tele-snaps to artists on spec in the hope of attracting business from them. Many of his clients were BBC programme makers who found his photographs useful records of their work.

In 1951, Cura came once again to the attention of the BBC's lawyers when he requested that he be allowed to photograph entire BBC productions, writing that his service "enables you to have a permanent pictorial record for valuable reference in years to come, of series which have a brief life of an hour or so and are then lost forever".<ref>Bignell, ''John Cura – Photographer of the Lost Archive'', p. 13.</ref> The BBC had also been contacted by several newspapers at this time, looking for permission to use Cura's tele-snaps—especially after it transpired that Cura had taken the only image of [[Oxford University Boat Club|Oxford]]'s boat sinking during [[The Boat Race 1951|that year's Boat Race]] between Oxford and [[Cambridge University Boat Club|Cambridge]]. The BBC made petitions to the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Houses of Parliament]] to have the [[Copyright law of the United Kingdom|Copyright Acts]] overhauled to give them [[legal certainty]] regarding the issue. Although a revised Copyright Bill was enacted in 1956, it did little to curtail Cura's activities.

Cura's business was at its peak in the mid-fifties, his business having doubled overnight following the launch of [[ITV Network|ITV]] in 1955. A second television set was purchased and a second camera constructed to enable Cura to photograph both channels. Cura also enjoyed success with two best-selling books on improving television reception and correcting picture faults, which were illustrated with his tele-snaps. He also appeared on the BBC's television panel game show ''[[What's My Line?]]''. Celebrity clients of the tele-snaps service included [[Benny Hill]] and the [[Beverley Sisters]]. By 1959, Cura claimed to have taken over 250,000 tele-snaps and that sets of his tele-snaps had been "presented to and graciously accepted by the [[British Royal Family|Royal Family]]; Their Majesties the [[Frederik IX of Denmark|King of Denmark]]; the late [[Haakon VII of Norway|King of Norway]]; [[Juliana of the Netherlands|Queen Juliana of the Netherlands]]; Ex-president [[Vincent Auriol|Auriol]] of France; [[Clement Attlee|Earl Attlee]]; Sir [[Winston Churchill]]; Mr [[Charlie Chaplin|Charles Chaplin]]; Mrs [[Eleanor Roosevelt]]"<ref>Bignell, ''John Cura – Photographer of the Lost Archive'', p. 14.</ref> as well as a wide range of newspapers and periodicals. However, when Cura raised the prices for his service in 1964, the BBC ordered a review of the tele-snap service, which at this stage was costing them £1,300 per annum, and, with many programmes now routinely recorded on film or video, the business began to decline.

John Cura continued to take tele-snaps right up within a few months of his death in 1969 from [[colorectal cancer|colon cancer]]. His widow offered her late husband's collection of tele-snaps to the BBC but was turned down. It is believed that they were subsequently destroyed.<ref>"Emily [Cura's widow] told us that when John died she got in touch with the BBC and said, "I've got a garage full of photos, do you want them?" and an executive said, "We're moving forward, Mrs Cura, not backwards." Emily told us she was so upset that she destroyed the lot." – Teddie Beverley, quoted in Lewisohn, ''John Cura: Snapshots of History''.</ref> However, many copies of tele-snaps survive on broadcasters' production files and in the private collections of many of the artists and technicians whose work Cura photographed.

==Cultural significance==
In the early days of television, the means of making recordings of television programmes were limited and programmes were, in the main, transmitted live. This began to change as techniques for recording programmes onto film ([[telerecording]]) and, later, [[videotape]] were developed in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lost-british-television.blogspot.com/2007/01/above-image-is-historic.html|title=The First TV Recordings|access-date=22 March 2007|last=Henderson|first=Andy|date=20 January 2007|publisher=Lost British Television}}{{Dead link|date=September 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref> Even after the technology for recording programmes had become the norm, it was a common practice, due to a combination of the costs of storage and restrictions on broadcasting repeats, for UK broadcasters to [[Lost television broadcast#Wiping|wipe]] programmes after transmission.<ref>{{cite book|last=Fiddy|first=Dick|title=Missing Believed Wiped. Searching for the lost treasures of British Television|year=2001|publisher=British Film Institute|location=London|isbn=0-85170-866-8|pages=5–10|chapter=Background}}</ref> As a result, John Cura's tele-snaps are often the only surviving record of many [[List of lost television broadcasts|lost programmes from the early years of television]].

Tele-snaps have been used to reconstruct lost television shows by marrying up the tele-snaps with audio recordings of missing shows to create a slide-show backed by the programme's soundtrack. Most notably, this technique has been employed, on an amateur, not-for-profit basis, by some enthusiasts of the British science fiction series ''[[Doctor Who]]'', which has nearly a hundred missing episodes.<ref>{{cite journal|editor1-last=Robinson|editor1-first=Bruce|editor2-last=Franks|editor2-first=Robert|date=10 May 1998|title=History of the Reconstructions Part I|journal=The Disused Yeti|issue=12|url=http://archive.whoniversity.co.uk/dy/is12.htm#12.1|access-date=20 March 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927023344/http://archive.whoniversity.co.uk/dy/is12.htm|archive-date=27 September 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|editor1-last=Robinson|editor1-first=Bruce|editor2-last=Franks|editor2-first=Robert|date=11 July 1998|title=History of the Reconstructions Part II|journal=The Disused Yeti|issue=13|url=http://archive.whoniversity.co.uk/dy/is13.htm#13.1|access-date=20 March 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927023324/http://archive.whoniversity.co.uk/dy/is13.htm|archive-date=27 September 2007}}</ref> Some professional reconstructions using tele-snaps have also been created, including:
* A brief (15-minute) reconstruction of episodes two and three of the ''Doctor Who'' serial ''[[The Ice Warriors]]'' for its VHS videotape release in 1998.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/ice.htm|title=The Ice Warriors|access-date=18 March 2007|last=Roberts|first=Steve|date=7 August 1998|work=Doctor Who Restoration Team|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071121043523/http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/ice.htm|archive-date=21 November 2007}}</ref>
* A full reconstruction of the final episode of the ''Doctor Who'' serial ''[[The Tenth Planet]]'' for its VHS videotape release in 2000.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/cybermen.htm|title='The Cybermen' Boxset|access-date=18 March 2007|last1=Roberts|first1=Steve|last2=Montagu|first2=Ralph|date=November 2000|work=Doctor Who Restoration Team|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071120110901/http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/cybermen.htm|archive-date=20 November 2007}}</ref>
* A full reconstruction of the ''Doctor Who'' serial ''[[The Power of the Daleks]]'' for the MP3 CD release of that story in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/doctorwho/news/cult/news/drwho/2005/06/08/19855.shtml|title=Doctor Who: News: Power of the Daleks|access-date=18 March 2007|date=8 June 2005|work=BBC – Official Doctor Who site}}</ref> This reconstruction was later included in the DVD release of an animated version of the serial in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.doctorwho.tv/news/?article=the-power-of-the-daleks-dvd-artwork-and-extras-unveiled|title=The Power of the Daleks DVD artwork and extras unveiled|last=McEwan|first=Cameron K|date=26 October 2016|website=Doctor Who|access-date=14 February 2021}}</ref>
*Similar full reconstructions of all four episodes of ''[[The Macra Terror]]'', episodes 2,4,5 and 6 of ''[[The Faceless Ones]]'', all six episodes of ''[[Fury from the Deep]]'', episode 3 of ''[[The Web of Fear]]'', all six episodes of ''[[The Power of the Daleks]]'' and episodes 1 & 3-7 of ''[[The Evil of the Daleks]]'' (with the surviving parts represented by the original episodes and surviving footage) have also been included in the subsequent DVD releases of the animated versions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.doctorwho.tv/news/?article=the-macra-terror-dvd-and-bluray-cover-art-and-special-features-revealed|title='The Macra Terror' DVD and Blu-Ray cover art and special features revealed|last=Dee|first=Christel|date=2 March 2019|website=Doctor Who|access-date=14 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.doctorwho.tv/news/?article=the-faceless-ones-dvd-bluray-reveal|title='The Faceless Ones' cover art and special features revealed|date=8 February 2020|website=Doctor Who|access-date=14 February 2021}}</ref>
* A condensed (30-minute) reconstruction of the seven-part ''Doctor Who'' serial ''[[Marco Polo (Doctor Who)|Marco Polo]]'' for the DVD release, "The Beginning", in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/beginningdvd.htm|title=The Beginning – DVD Boxset|access-date=18 March 2007|last1=Roberts|first1=Steve|last2=Ayres|first2=Mark|date=15 November 2005|work=Doctor Who Restoration Team|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061230063259/http://www.purpleville.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/rtwebsite/beginningdvd.htm|archive-date=30 December 2006}}</ref>
* A condensed reconstruction of the missing episodes of the 1961 science fiction serial ''[[A for Andromeda]]'' for its DVD release in 2006. Since at the time of release no soundtrack for the missing episodes of this serial existed, this reconstruction is backed by music used in the serial with on-screen captions employed to narrate the story.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dvdtimes.co.uk/content.php?contentid=62660|title=The Andromeda Anthology – Review|access-date=18 March 2007|last=Couzens|first=Gary|date=2 September 2006|work=DVD Times}}</ref> The full soundtrack of the partially-existing episode 7 was subsequently recovered.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}
* Narrated reconstructions of episodes from the first season of ''[[The Avengers (TV series)|The Avengers]]'' have been included as extras on the Region 2 DVDs of the series released by Optimum.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://declassified.theavengers.tv/keel_reconstructions.htm|title=The Avengers Reconstructed|access-date=29 May 2011|last=Hayes|first=Alan|work=The Avengers Declassified|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110814111506/http://declassified.theavengers.tv/keel_reconstructions.htm|archive-date=14 August 2011}}</ref>
